content: Rabies elimination is considered a global public good due to its significant impact on public health and its alignment with the One Health approach. Efforts will be made to assist countries in integrating rabies elimination programs with other healthcare initiatives, thereby strengthening health systems and improving outcomes for other diseases. Guidance will also be provided to countries on how to approach development partners for financial support, enabling them to take ownership and implement local programs to achieve their elimination goals. Effective and efficient use of financial and other resources is critical to achieving the Zero by 30 goal, which aims to eliminate human deaths from dog-mediated rabies by 2030. Existing models for vaccine forecasting and investment have been adapted to predict resource needs accurately. Program outcomes will be used to advocate for further investment and to establish clear strategies for resource mobilization. Monitoring and evaluation of work plans are essential to refine and improve implementation in subsequent countries and phases. Financing strategies for the activities outlined in the global strategic plan are detailed in the budget, and collaboration with experienced external fundraisers will help generate investments for elimination efforts. Innovative funding mechanisms and synergies with other programs will also be explored. The United Against Rabies collaboration will regularly monitor and report on the results and impact of its activities to key stakeholders. Advocacy at global, regional, and national levels will promote investment in rabies elimination. Lessons learned from the first phase of implementation will inform and refine subsequent phases, ensuring continuous improvement and progress toward the goal of Zero by 30. The phased approach to rabies elimination involves three stages: Start-Up (2018–2020), Scale-Up (2021–2025), and Mop-Up (2026–2030). The Start-Up phase focuses on building a strong foundation by preparing tools and structures to catalyze action, engaging countries where rabies is a priority, and developing national and regional elimination plans. The Scale-Up phase expands efforts to include most endemic countries, leveraging the foundation established in the first phase. The Mop-Up phase targets the remaining countries, ensuring that all regions are engaged in the fight against rabies and that the final steps toward elimination are achieved. The budget for Phase 1 includes capacity-building to support countries in developing robust elimination strategies, advocacy to prioritize rabies elimination, and the establishment of harmonized global norms and standards. Countries will use their national plans to mobilize domestic and international resources for financing and implementing control activities. Investing in rabies elimination strengthens health systems, improves equity and access to healthcare, and contributes to sustainable development. Governance of the United Against Rabies collaboration will involve a Global Steering Group (GSG) composed of representatives from partner organizations, including WHO, OIE, FAO, and GARC. The GSG will also engage external experts and stakeholders as needed to support evidence-based decision-making. Monitoring progress and managing risks are integral to the success of the global strategic plan. Countries are at the core of the plan, with primary responsibility for implementing activities detailed in their national rabies elimination plans. Regular reporting, evaluation, and sharing of lessons learned will guide adjustments to activities and budgets for subsequent phases. Reaching Zero by 30 will save lives, reduce the economic burden on vulnerable rural communities, and prevent the suffering caused by this preventable disease. Investing in rabies elimination not only addresses a fatal but preventable disease but also builds capacity in neglected regions and improves access to health services. The time to act is now, leveraging existing knowledge, tools, and technology to achieve the goal of Zero by 30.
